summary:
Loreto is a department of Peru and stands under the national framework: Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

No trans-specific regional law, ordinance, police directive or enforcement finding for Loreto appears in the sources. Every attached item is national in scope, and as national law the restrictions below apply in Loreto.

Facility access is restricted by statute. On 2 April 2025 the Congress plenary approved, exempt from a second vote, the dictamen of the law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents, whose article 5 bars from public sanitary facilities anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex. Exceptions are limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs.

An earlier stage of the same package drew unanimous approval in the Congress Commission on Women and Family on 20 February 2025, covering bills 6506 and 8457, which would bar entry to public sanitary facilities destined to the sex opposite to one's birth sex. That version set exceptions for custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and required unambiguous signage. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory and warned that security staff would judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their DNI.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report recorded 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women the most affected and hate crimes rising; a 2024 report's co-author, the trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, stated that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The report recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of the trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang, with bodies showing gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting indicating extreme hate.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the bathroom statute does not meet.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, found that article 5 conditions basic rights on verifiable biological sex and implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute had already documented dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu, and the same analysis notes that Congress banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage.

The restriction reaches private life as well as public facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

The April 2025 legislative package also bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity', removing the visual markers a trans visitor might otherwise use to identify affirming spaces.
localsOnly:
In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings.

In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Congress has repeatedly foreclosed statutory protection: inclusive language was banned in the same legislative package and equal marriage was rejected again.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any departmental ordinance, regional police directive or facility-signage practice specific to Loreto exists is unresolved; the sources contain no Loreto-level instrument and the record rests entirely on national law.

The relationship between bills 6506 and 8457 and article 5 of the April 2025 law is not resolved here. The sources document the February 2025 committee approval awaiting plenary backing and the 2 April 2025 plenary approval of the sexual-integrity law separately, without stating whether the bills were enacted as distinct statutes.

Whether the DNI-check practice Gianna Camacho warned of, or any enforcement action under article 5, has been recorded in Loreto is not sourced. Nor are figures on facility refusals, complaints or prosecutions nationally.

The final disposition of the dismissed gym complaint on appeal, and whether the televised harassment of Susel Paredes attracted any regulator or employer sanction, are not sourced.
